entries.title: Families call for criminal charges for South Chicago Chapel owners at vigil
entries.summary: <p>Cecelia Palmer was in charge of her sister-in-law’s funeral arrangements earlier this year. Now, she looks back and agonizes about her decision.</p><p>Palmer’s sister-in-law Nicole Williams-Smith was supposedly cremated after her services at South Chicago Chapel, but when her family received the ashes, Palmer said it looked more like a pile of dirt and rocks.</p><p>“What are these?” Palmer said, looking at a photo of the alleged ashes the funeral home gave her. “Are they even human remains?”</p><p>Palmer is now joining the growing number of loved ones demanding answers from the funeral home and city and state officials about what actually happened the remains of their deceased friends and family. Around 25 people gathered at a vigil Sunday evening at the South Chicago Chapel to release balloons and call for criminal charges in the case.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dd0000" name="image-dd0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4bb411/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/44a8bbf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a40f139/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Cecelia Palmer, Nicole Williams-Smith's sister-in-law, was among the relatives and supporters attending a vigil Sunday outside South Chicago Chapel, where dozens of decomposing bodies and unidentified remains were found earlier this month. The funeral home was shut down. Palmer said when she received her sister-in-law's remains, she questioned whether that's what they reallty were - they looked like rocks, she said." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a40f139/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a864c81/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a40f139/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8400x4714+0+443/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F28%2Ff89cf335465f81b699edcffda8fa%2Fsouth-chi-chapel-vigil-5.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cecelia Palmer, who was among those attending the vigil Sunday, shows a picture on her phone of the remains of her sister-in-law Nicole Williams-Smith, which she received from South Chicago Chapel. She questioned whether that’s what they really were — they looked like rocks, she said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Please, city officials, please step up and do your job,” said Lisette Guillen, executive director of Case Files Chicago. “We need criminal charges on this matter because this behavior is horrific and criminal.”</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>state shut down</u></a> South Chicago Chapel earlier this month after receiving a tip that owners Clark and Johanna Morgan were improperly storing bodies. Inside the funeral home, investigators found 56 bodies in various stages of decomposition. For months neighbors complained about the smell coming from the building.</p><p>“Was she among those?” Palmer said. “I’ve called and left messages with everybody, emails, so far haven’t heard.”</p><p>It <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" target="_blank" ><u>wasn’t the first time</u></a> the couple was accused of mishandling remains. Last year, a Chicago Heights Crematory owned by the Morgans was shut down.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a She said she’s filed more than 30 complaints with government agencies about the incident.</p><p>Hearing the news of the dozens of decomposing bodies at South Chicago Chapel was heartbreaking, Kristofek said, but she found some solace because she was no longer alone in the experience and it’s started gaining public attention, she said.</p><p>“It was a relief because there was other people. When you bury them, when you cremate them, you get the ashes, so you have a peace about that. entries.title: The anatomy of Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong's potential MVP season
entries.summary: <p>As hot as Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong is, it’s easy to forget how cold he was.</p><p>Through 50 games, Crow-Armstrong was hitting .225 with an OPS of .659. He had five home runs and 20 RBI. The Cubs were halfway through what became a 10-game losing streak, and manager Craig Counsell was looking for answers.</p><p>After Crow-Armstrong homered in the next game, Counsell moved him from the bottom of the order to the top — the very top.</p><p>“When we moved Pete there, honestly, we needed a jump,” Counsell said. “We were struggling scoring runs, and we were looking for a spark. It wasn’t very analytical. Now I look at the lineup, and he just comes around more.”</p><p>Slowly but surely, Crow-Armstrong began to produce. He got hot in June, hitting 10 home runs in the first 18 games of the month. But it wasn’t until the Cubs’ trip that month to New York to face the Mets that Crow-Armstrong’s season completely changed.</p><p>The way bench coach Ryan Flaherty tells it, Crow-Armstrong was working in the batting cage at Citi Field with assistant hitting coach John Mallee. After his eighth swing, Crow-Armstrong walked out of the cage and essentially said, “I found something that I’m going to be able to repeat for a long time.”</p><p>“He’s a pretty honest kid,” Flaherty told the Sun-Times. “And here we are, two months after that, and he was right on.”</p><p>Entering the game Sunday night against the Reds, Crow-Armstrong was hitting .282 with an OPS of .944, 36 homers — to which he added a leadoff blast Sunday — and 90 RBI. According to wins above replacement, he was the most valuable player in baseball, with marks of 9.1 from Fangraphs and 8.3 from Baseball Reference.</p><p>And he’s the odds-on favorite to win the National League Most Valuable Player Award.</p><p>What the heck happened?</p><p>“It’s just the natural progression of a season,” Crow-Armstrong told the Sun-Times. “I’ve known that I’m capable of this. Obviously, there’s swing changes you can make. I definitely freed myself up by lowering the hands and creating a different kind of rhythm for myself and then implementing the leg kick.</p><p>“Getting on the dish against lefties really helped me learn the strike zone better. But then not feeling like I’m in any rush to get to two strikes. Once I’m there, I still feel like I can control the zone while also looking to do damage.”</p><p>Just last year, Crow-Armstrong occasionally would bunt with two strikes to try to make something happen. Now, 10 of his 37 homers have come with two strikes. Everyone knew he was a defensive phenom, thanks to his speed and athleticism. But the extent of his power has surprised most — but not him.</p><p>“That’s another thing that I’ve always had in me,” he said. “Even when I was in high school, I was kind of slappy, could go the other way really well. I just didn’t know how to pull the ball efficiently. Some swings I’d take I can remember like, Oh, I’ve got that in me, and then I just wouldn’t be able to translate it to the game.</p><p>“John Mallee made it make sense to me that my swing works in that way and I should take advantage of it. So the goal now is the opposite of who I thought I used to be, which was I want my direction to go to left-center so that when I’m early, I can pull the ball.</p><p>“Nah, man. I’m pulling everything you throw at me. That’s my goal. That’s what has helped me start moving really efficiently.”</p><p>Counsell said he knew Crow-Armstrong would hit home runs. It was just a matter of learning how to do it.</p><p>“He was a very young player to the big leagues,” Counsell said of Crow-Armstrong, who made his big-league debut shortly after turning 21. “It’s hard to be able to get the ball in the air to the pull side and have good pitch discipline. Those are two counter things, really, because you have to hit the ball out front, and that means you have to make a decision a little bit sooner.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong also is proving you don’t need to be big and burly to put a ball into the bleachers.</p><p>“He’s very wiry strong,” Flaherty said. “Pound for pound, I bet he’s one of the stronger guys on the team. You watch him in the weight room, he’s strong. He looks the way he does, but he has the ability to create an absurd amount of force in a short period of time, which I think is where that power comes from. It’s always been there.”</p><p>And it doesn’t appear to be going anywhere.</p><p>“Every time he’s coming to bat right now, it’s like something special’s about to happen,” Flaherty said. “You think he isn’t going to do it again, and he does it again.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs stand behind Shota Imanaga after he allows three homers in loss to Reds
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs have a Shota Imanaga problem, but they’re not ready to admit it.</p><p>The left-hander allowed three home runs Sunday night in a 7-5 loss to the Reds, marking the sixth time this season he has allowed at least three in a game. That’s a record for a franchise that celebrated its 150th year this weekend.</p><p>“He gave up three homers, and two had men on base,” manager Craig Counsell said. “The math doesn’t really work there as far as having a good start. We know Shota is going to give up some home runs. That’s the nature of his repertoire. Three in a start, that’s too many.”</p><p>At least Imanaga lasted longer than the two innings he pitched in his last start a week before in Seattle. But the Cubs overcame that to win 19-2. They gave themselves a chance against Reds ace Chase Burns, taking a 2-0 lead into the fourth, but the offense was too little, too late.</p><p>Imanaga allowed a three-run homer to Hector Rodriguez (his fourth homer of the season), a solo shot to Dane Myers (his sixth) and a two-run shot to Tyler Stephenson on a pitch out of the strike zone, making it 6-3 in the fifth.</p><p>“The mistake pitches that I can’t throw end up in zones that they’re going to hit,” Imanaga said through a translator. “And here, those swings don’t end up in singles; those end up in home runs. There’s a lot of frustration within myself. But I need to be the one to figure it out.”</p><p>Counsell pushed back on the suggestion that Imanaga’s rotation spot is in jeopardy.</p><p>“He’s not having a bad season,” Counsell said. “He’s having a pretty decent season. I wouldn’t say that at all, no. We need Shota. We need Shota to be good for us. So we have to work at helping him be better.”</p><h3>Davis, Lester get blue jackets</h3><p>Former Cubs catcher Jody Davis and pitcher Jon Lester were inducted into the Cubs’ Hall of Fame and received their blue jackets in pregame ceremonies.</p><p>Davis was a two-time All-Star in eight seasons with the Cubs, including 1984, when the team won the National League East for its first postseason appearance in 39 years.</p><p>Lester also was a two-time All-Star in five full seasons with the Cubs, but his postseason achievement was more notable. He helped the 2016 team end the club’s 108-year World Series-championship drought.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The Cubs released 2020 first-round pick (16th overall) and Chicago native Ed Howard from Triple-A Iowa on Saturday. Between Iowa and Double-A Knoxville this season, the shortstop was hitting .168 with a .469 OPS and two homers in 52 games.</p><p>• Right-hander Edward Cabrera (blister on middle finger) is scheduled to begin a rehab assignment Tuesday at Iowa.</p><h3>On deck</h3><p><b>BREWERS AT CUBS</b></p><p><b>Monday:</b> Kyle Harrison (10-3, 2.79 ERA) vs. Clay Holmes (5-6, 2.26), 6:40 p.m., Marquee, 670-AM, 104.3-FM.</p><p><b>Tuesday:</b> Robert Gasser (4-5, 4.59) vs. Matthew Boyd (8-3, 3.99), 6:40 p.m., Marquee, 670-AM, 104.3-FM.</p><p><b>Wednesday:</b> Jacob Misiorowski (14-5, 1.73) vs. David Peterson (7-7, 5.11), 6:40 p.m., Marquee, 670-AM, 104.3-FM.</p><p><b>Thursday:</b> Logan Henderson (9-2, 2.48) vs. Kevin Gausman (8-11, 4.52), 6:15 p.m., Fox 32, 670-AM, 104.3-FM.<br></p>
